codes.definition: Chip and server energy for the call multiplied by grid carbon intensity at run time (§8.5–§8.6)
Cooling, power conversion and other data-center overhead, derived from OPE and the facility PUE
The call’s share of the model’s total training emissions, amortized over lifetime token throughput
The call’s share of manufacturing and construction emissions for the accelerators, servers and facility it used
Training or fine-tuning run on the Subscriber’s own infrastructure, measured by the infra agent and attributed 100% to that Subscriber
Published or estimated lifecycle training emissions for a model version, with source citation (Appendix A)
Expected total tokens served by a model version over its deployment life
Manufacturing emissions per server or accelerator, including a configurable share for networking and facility construction
Expected service life of the hardware class
Share of hardware time doing useful work; from GPU (§21.2) where measured, otherwise a provider default
Accelerator time consumed by the call, measured or modeled from tokens and model class
OPE + FAC + TRA + EMB (+ STE where applicable), always stored with its component split
Lifecycle emissions per functional unit, using Useful Output Count (UOC, §21.2) as the unit

Cradle-to-gate emissions for one component class of a device. Component classes use the OpenTelemetry hw.type values (cpu, gpu, memory, physical_disk, network, power_supply, enclosure), extended where needed with accelerator subcomponents (logic die, HBM stack, package and substrate, board)
Source of each EMC value: manufacturer PCF (ISO 14067), open model (e.g., Boavizta), peer-reviewed literature, or default
Substance and material composition per IEC 62474, including critical raw materials, where the manufacturer provides it
Logic die area and fabrication node, used for fab-based estimates when no PCF exists
High-bandwidth memory capacity per accelerator, the input for memory-scaled embodied estimates
Date the device entered service
Planned service life before decommissioning (typically 2–6 years)
Service life at decommissioning
Sum of EMC divided by (service life in hours × HUR); supersedes the single HEE value where component data exists
Reduction in D-EMH from extending service life beyond RCP
Mass captured per reporting interval
% of CO2 in input stream actually captured
Actual throughput vs. rated nameplate capacity
Operational hours vs. downtime, with reason code
Running total mass captured, resets per crediting period
Destination: geologic, mineralization, utilization, transport
Purity of captured CO2 output stream
Loss during compression, transport, or injection
Total energy used per tonne captured
Breakdown of grid, renewable, and onsite generation
Water used per tonne captured
Chemical media used per tonne captured
Number of sorbent/solvent regeneration cycles
Last calibration date and certification status of metering hardware
Direct-metered vs. estimated/modeled
Applicable third-party standard (Puro.earth, Verra, Isometric, etc.)
Unique identifier for the capture facility or project
Latitude/longitude of facility
Cadence at which this Provider reports
ML-estimated efficiency where direct sensing is unavailable
Forecasted captured mass for current crediting period
Flags telemetry readings outside expected operational bounds
Composite confidence score for a record's reliability
Uncertainty band on any derived (D-) estimate
Identifier for the ML feature set used to generate a derived record
Adjusts captured-mass credit based on energy source mix
Tier of the model serving the call (frontier, mid, small), from the provider/model lookup in §9.4
Output-quality parity when a sampled prompt is re-run on a smaller or cheaper model tier, vs. the production model
Input tokens divided by output tokens
Share of input tokens that repeat unchanged system prompts or prior-turn context
Share of input tokens served from the provider’s prompt cache
Share of calls regenerated, retried, or discarded without use
Completed tasks or accepted responses (the denominator for efficiency)
Mean GPU/accelerator utilization over the interval
Provisioned but unused compute over the interval
Latency-tolerant calls executed synchronously instead of batched
Carbon intensity of the grid for the region and hour the call ran (§8.6)
Difference between GCI at run time and the lowest GCI available within the job’s allowed window
Normalized from MFP and MTR; 100 = smallest adequate model in use
Normalized from TIO, CXB, CHR and RTR
Normalized from GPU, IDC and BTC
Normalized from GCI and CWD
Weighted composite of the four sub-scores (§21.4)
Useful outputs (UOC) per dollar of AI spend
Useful outputs per kWh
Useful outputs per kg CO2e
Projected monthly $, kWh and kg CO2e reduction if open recommendations are applied
UTC start and end of the energy use the record covers; long jobs are split into sub-intervals no longer than the finest factor resolution available
Time resolution of each factor applied: realtime (≤5 min), hourly, daily, monthly or annual
Start and end of the period each factor value applies to, so it can be checked against IVL
Whether each factor was measured at the time, forecast at decision time, or a historical average
Tariff period in effect when energy was used: off-peak, mid-peak, on-peak, super-off-peak, critical-peak, or real-time
Energy price applied to the interval, from the operator’s tariff or a price signal
Peak-demand rate in the applicable tariff and its measurement window (e.g., highest 15-minute average in the billing month)
This workload’s power draw during the interval that set the billing-period peak, or during the coincident-peak window
Which signal produced GCI (§21.2): marginal or average, and the provider (e.g., WattTime, Electricity Maps, grid operator)
Lowest forecast intensity and its start time within the job’s allowed window, as forecast when the scheduling decision was made
Renewable energy curtailed in the grid region during the interval, where the grid operator publishes it
Delay the workload owner declared acceptable before the job was scheduled
Granularity at which any claimed renewable or carbon-free supply was matched to consumption: hourly, monthly or annual, with the certificate reference (EAC, §22.4)
Energy × (intensity at the requested time − intensity at the actual run time), using the same GSG and FTR for both
Energy × (TRT at the requested time − TRT at the actual run time), plus any change in D-DCC
PKD × DMD allocated to the workload; reported separately from energy cost
Share of shifted energy consumed during intervals with RCF > 0
Share of a workload’s energy whose carbon factor had hourly or finer resolution (FTR) and an overlapping FVW
Tier the router first chose: cache, micro, workhorse, or frontier. The tier that finally served the call stays in MTR (§21.2)
Why that tier was chosen: cache hit, hard rule, classifier, carbon or thermal override, user or policy pin, or escalation
The router’s calibrated probability that the selected tier meets the quality floor
Time spent in Tier 0 and Tier 1 before dispatch to a model
Energy used by the routing step itself; measured where the router has its own host, otherwise modeled from RCL and host power
Whether the response came from an exact or semantic cache, with the similarity score of the match
Latency limit declared for the workload class; a hard constraint on the routing decision
The energy price λ applied to the decision: tariff plus internal carbon price × grid intensity, scaled by thermal pressure (§21.8.2)
Whether a lower tier was aborted and re-routed upward, and the trigger: entropy, validation failure, timeout, or user regenerate
Tokens the aborted tier generated before escalation
Energy spent on the aborted attempt, charged to the routing decision rather than hidden
Mean token entropy over the first k output tokens of the lower tier; the main escalation signal
Whether the call was sampled for opt-in shadow evaluation on another tier (§21.4)
Version of the router model, thresholds, weights and quality judge in effect, so every decision can be audited and reproduced
Counterfactual energy had the call run on the default tier, minus actual energy including RCE and EWE
Total router energy (RCE) divided by gross energy saved before router cost. Design invariant: at or below 0.05
Share of down-tiered calls that escalated
Expected calibration error of RPS measured against shadow-evaluation outcomes
Share of shadow-sampled, down-tiered calls whose output fell below the parity threshold and was not escalated
Instantaneous board power of the accelerator (NVIDIA DCGM/NVML, AMD SMI, Intel XPU Manager, or cloud runtime equivalent)
Cumulative energy from the device’s hardware counter; preferred over integrating APW
Enforced power cap and the default cap, so deliberate power capping can be credited as an efficiency action
Compute and memory clocks against their maximums
Active causes limiting clocks (power cap, GPU or memory thermal, hardware slowdown) and time spent throttled
Core and memory (HBM) temperatures and the device’s slowdown threshold
Share of time compute units and tensor pipes are actually active. A truer utilization measure than kernel-busy time, which reports a device as fully busy whenever any kernel runs
Share of time the device memory interface is busy. Token generation is usually memory-bound, so this predicts per-token energy
Accelerator memory in use against capacity
Accelerator-to-accelerator (NVLink, Infinity Fabric, ICI) and PCIe traffic
Correctable and uncorrectable memory errors, retired or remapped memory rows, and fatal device errors
Hardware partition serving the workload (MIG slice, vGPU profile, or whole device) and its share, used to apportion device energy among tenants
Requests waiting to be scheduled on the replica
Share of key-value cache blocks in use; high values precede preemption and wasted recomputation
Sequences in the running batch; larger batches lower energy per token
Latency to the first output token, dominated by prompt processing. Server-side where available, client-side from the chat plugin otherwise
Mean time between output tokens during generation
Precision of the deployed model’s weights and activations (BF16, FP8, INT8, INT4, FP4)
Share of draft tokens accepted by the target model where speculative decoding is used
Whole-server input power, including CPUs, memory, fans, network cards and power-supply losses (DMTF Redfish, IPMI DCMI)
CPU and DRAM energy from RAPL counters, collected through Kepler or a node exporter
Fan speed as a share of maximum. Fan power rises steeply with speed, so this signals air-cooling overhead
Power-supply output divided by input
Measured rack draw against provisioned capacity
Total facility energy divided by IT energy over the interval (ISO/IEC 30134-2). Replaces annual defaults in FAC (§8.8.1) where available
Site water use divided by IT energy (ISO/IEC 30134-9). Replaces water defaults (§4.3) where available
Server or rack inlet temperature, judged against the ASHRAE recommended envelope
Liquid-cooling supply and return temperatures and flow rate at the coolant distribution unit
Remaining cooling capacity of the hall or loop
Ambient wet-bulb temperature at the site. It drives chiller efficiency and evaporative water use, so it forecasts PUE and WUE
Whether a grid demand-response or curtailment event is active for the site, and the reduction requested (OpenADR)

Measured energy per token, split into prompt processing and generation, for each model × hardware × precision × batch-size band. Built from AEC or NPW and token counts. Replaces modeled per-token rates (§8.7) where available and feeds the router (§21.8.2)
Composite of throttled time (ATR), temperature margin to slowdown (ATM) and cooling headroom (CHD). Raises the router’s energy price for that pool
Predicted remaining reliable life from ERR trends, thermal history and age. Feeds refresh decisions (RCP, §8.8.8) and the lifecycle record (§22.8)
Provisioned but unused power capacity (from RKP); the facility counterpart of idle compute (IDC, §21.2)
Unique identifier of a registered sensor type
What is measured, as a QUDT quantity-kind identifier (power, temperature, flow, and so on)
UCUM unit code, such as W, Cel or L/min
Component, device, node, rack, row, hall, site, or grid
Stated accuracy, which sets the reading’s confidence tier (§8.1–§8.3); calibration is tracked with SCT (§20.5)
Native sampling period and how readings are aggregated (mean, max, or counter delta)

Solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, or storage discharge
Balancing area or market zone of the generator, for deliverability matching

Water treated, recycled, or remediated for reuse

Water stress rating of the watershed (e.g., WRI Aqueduct)
Thermal energy delivered to an external user
Temperature of exported heat
District heating, greenhouse, industry, or buildings
Reused energy divided by total facility energy (ISO/IEC 30134-6)
Fuel or heat source the exported heat replaces
Mass of material recovered for reuse or recycling
Plastic, metals, electronics, batteries, other
Reference tracing material from source to recycler
R2, e-Stewards, or equivalent
Emissions avoided by displacing the DFB heat source with HEX
Water benefit computed with the VWBA method
Emissions avoided versus virgin material production
Manufacturer, model, part number and serial number, taken from DMTF Redfish inventory or the operator’s asset system and mapped to OTel host.* attributes
In service, redeployed, refurbished, parts harvested, recycled, or disposed
When the asset entered its current state
Organization holding the asset: operator, refurbisher, broker, or recycler
Internal reuse, resale, donation, or parts recovery
Share of the asset’s mass recovered for reuse or recycling at end of life
Operator-reported, refurbisher- or recycler-certified, manufacturer take-back, or inferred
Share of decommissioned hardware, by mass, reused or recycled rather than disposed, reported in line with ISO 59020
